# Export


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

The Arduino UNO Q runs models with
[llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp), which loads GGUF
files. This notebook turns the fine-tuned Qwen3.5 0.8B from
[Fine-tuning](06_finetune.ipynb), trained on 199 examples, into GGUF
files at 8 and 4 bits, and scores each one on the test set through
llama.cpp. The scores must match the MLX model’s before a file goes to
the board.

## Merging the adapter

mlx-lm’s own GGUF export supports only Llama, Mistral and Mixtral
models, so the GGUF file comes from llama.cpp’s converter,
`convert_hf_to_gguf.py`. The converter reads checkpoints in the Hugging
Face layout. The mlx-community checkpoint we trained on is not in that
layout: its tensor names start with `language_model.model.` instead of
`model.language_model.`, its vision encoder is removed, and its
convolution weights are transposed.

The adapter changes only linear projections, and the base weights of
those 124 projections are identical in the two checkpoints.
[`fuse_lora`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/export.html#fuse_lora)
therefore merges the adapter into the original `Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B`
checkpoint. It renames each adapted layer and adds `scale · Bᵀ·Aᵀ` to
its weight, the formula mlx-lm uses when it fuses. The other files of
the checkpoint are copied unchanged:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/export.py#L19"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### fuse_lora

``` python
def fuse_lora(
    base:str, # Directory of the original Hugging Face checkpoint
    adapters:str, # Directory of the mlx-lm adapters
    out:str, # Directory for the merged checkpoint
)->pathlib._local.Path:
```

*Merge mlx-lm LoRA adapters into a Hugging Face checkpoint*

We checked the merge by loading the merged checkpoint with mlx-lm: it
wrote the same messages as the adapter for the first three test records.

This cell merged the adapter and converted the result. It needs the
`export` extra (`pip install -e '.[export]'`), llama.cpp’s command-line
tools (`brew install llama.cpp`, version 0.8.0 here) and a checkout of
llama.cpp at the same commit for `convert_hf_to_gguf.py`, and does not
run in tests:

``` python
import subprocess, sys
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
LLAMA_CPP = Path('~/pro/dev/llama.cpp').expanduser()
run = Path('../models/qwen3.5-0.8b-n199')
hf = fuse_lora(snapshot_download('Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B'), run/'adapters', run/'hf')
gguf = run/'gguf'; gguf.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
bf16 = gguf/'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-bf16.gguf'
subprocess.run([sys.executable, LLAMA_CPP/'convert_hf_to_gguf.py', hf, '--outtype', 'bf16', '--outfile', bf16], env={'PYTHONPATH': str(LLAMA_CPP/'gguf-py')}, check=True)
for q in ('Q8_0', 'Q4_K_M'): subprocess.run(['llama-quantize', bf16, gguf/f'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-{q}.gguf', q], check=True)
```

## Scoring with llama.cpp

[`score_gguf`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/export.html#score_gguf)
sends each test record to a running `llama-server` and checks the
message. It builds the prompt with
[`student_input`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/baseline.html#student_input),
the same chat-formatted string the MLX runs used, and decodes greedily.
Any change in score therefore comes from llama.cpp and the quantization.
Each row also keeps llama.cpp’s token counts and timings:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/export.py#L43"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### score_gguf

``` python
async def score_gguf(
    url:str, # Address of a running `llama-server`
    rows:list, # Test rows with `id`, `tuple` and `record`
    tok, # The model's tokenizer, to build the chat-formatted prompt
    name:str, # Name of the GGUF file, saved in each row
    n_par:int=4, # Requests in flight at once
    max_tokens:int=400, # Longest message to generate
)->list: # One row per input, with the message, its checks and llama.cpp's timings
```

*Have a llama.cpp server write and check a message for each row*

This cell scored each file, with
`llama-server -m <file> --port 8091 -c 4096 -np 4` running in a
terminal. It does not run in tests:

``` python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from edgeslm.dataset import read_jsonl, write_jsonl
test = read_jsonl('../data/test-v1.jsonl')
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('../models/qwen3.5-0.8b-n199/hf')
q = 'Q4_K_M'  # restart the server with each file, then set q to match
write_jsonl(f'../data/gguf-v1-qwen3.5-0.8b-n199-{q}.jsonl', await score_gguf('http://localhost:8091', test, tok, f'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-{q}.gguf'))
```

Quantization costs no checks. The changed messages we read differ in
wording only, such as “no longer sees its leaves” for “has not seen its
leaves”. The number of messages identical to the MLX model’s shows how
many changed:

``` python
{k: sum(a['message'] == b['message'] for a, b in zip(v, runs['MLX bf16'])) for k, v in runs.items()}
```

    {'MLX bf16': 270, 'GGUF Q8_0': 265, 'GGUF Q4_K_M': 251}

The 4-bit file also writes the right marker for every item:

``` python
markers(runs['GGUF Q4_K_M'], test)
```

    Counter({('early', '👀'): 209, ('moderate', '⚠️'): 148, ('severe', '🚨'): 112})

The 4-bit file is 542 MB, against 834 MB for 8 bits and 1.56 GB for
bf16. It scores as well as the others, so it is the file for the UNO Q.
Speed and memory on the board are still to be measured.

## Running on the UNO Q

The colleague with the board needs llama.cpp built on it, the 4-bit file
`qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf`, and the folder `data/uno-q` from
this repo. The folder holds three test prompts, `prompt-N.txt`, already
in the model’s chat format, and the 4-bit file’s message for each,
`expected-N.txt`. This cell wrote them, and does not run in tests:

``` python
q4 = read_jsonl('../data/gguf-v1-qwen3.5-0.8b-n199-Q4_K_M.jsonl')
for i in range(3):
    Path(f'../data/uno-q/prompt-{i}.txt').write_text(student_input(tok, test[i]['record'], SHORT_PROMPT))
    Path(f'../data/uno-q/expected-{i}.txt').write_text(q4[i]['message'])
```

The steps below run on the board. First, build llama.cpp at the version
used here (0.8.0) on the board’s Debian:

``` sh
sudo apt install git cmake build-essential time
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
git checkout 8642541b2
cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j 4
```

The tools are in `build/bin`. Copy the GGUF file and the `uno-q` folder
next to them, then run each step from `build/bin`.

**Check the download.** The checksum must match before anything else:

``` sh
sha256sum qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf
# 4f283f2f87413fe1c3cdb83f226c8cdf3c31eae7dc456c268a702ba0a7c63769
```

A different value means the download is incomplete or the file has
changed. Download it again.

**Write a message.** This writes the message for the first test prompt
with greedy decoding, as the scoring did:

``` sh
./llama-completion -m qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf -f uno-q/prompt-0.txt -n 400 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -no-cnv --no-display-prompt
```

The output ends with `[end of text]`. Compare the text before it with
`uno-q/expected-0.txt`. On a Mac it is identical. The board computes on
a different processor, so a few words can change. A different marker,
location or number of paragraphs is a real problem: report it.

**Measure speed.** Test prompts average 168 tokens and messages 71, so
benchmark those sizes on the four cores:

``` sh
./llama-bench -m qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf -p 168 -n 71 -t 4
```

The table gives tokens per second for reading the prompt (`pp168`) and
for writing the message (`tg71`). The time for one message is about 168
÷ pp168 + 71 ÷ tg71 seconds.

**Measure memory.** Run the first step under GNU `time`:

``` sh
/usr/bin/time -v ./llama-completion -m qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf -f uno-q/prompt-0.txt -n 400 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -no-cnv --no-display-prompt
```

The line `Maximum resident set size` gives the peak memory in kilobytes.

Send back the three outputs, the `llama-bench` table and the peak
memory.

### Scoring all test records on the board

The scope requires final scores measured on the target board. If a
computer with this repo can reach the board over the network, the
colleague starts a server on the board:

``` sh
./llama-server -m qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8091 -c 4096
```

On the computer, run the scoring cell above with the board’s address,
`http://<board-ip>:8091`, and `n_par=1`, so that each timing measures
one message on its own. Each row then holds the board’s timings for that
message. We have not run this yet.
